_notes.purpose: The naming registers as DATA. One register is chosen per world, deterministically, from the world's own answers (xeric_forge_naming), and every pass that invents a proper noun carries it: the concept pass names the place off it, the places pass names the businesses off it, the cast pass names the people off it, and the deterministic gates replace repeat offenders FROM it. Hand-written banks are the whole point — good raw material is what lets a small model punch above its weight, and a model that copies a bank entry verbatim has not failed, it has used the library.
_notes.why: Eight worlds were forged before this file existed and Elias Thorne lived in every one of them; Thorne/Vane/Vance/Voss covered 27 of 32 surnames, six towns had a Rusty-something and five had a St. Jude's. Each forge pass is a separate model call with no memory of any other world, so every world independently converges on the statistically safest tokens. A register moves the whole distribution somewhere specific; twelve registers make twelve different somewheres.
_notes.shape: Each register: key, label (for the build log), sound (one line, quoted into prompts), given (first names, mixed gender, a whole lifetime's worth), family (surnames), toponyms (place-name material, usable as world names), businesses (full names over real doors), church (what the congregation actually calls it — St. Jude retired at five worlds). Banks are sized for a twelve-person cast with room left over; when one runs dry the code borrows from the other registers in rotation.
_notes.banned: The observed repeat offenders, by name. These are banned in prompts AND replaced by the deterministic gates — a prompt ban alone is a hope, not a gate. world_words are banned anywhere in a world's or place's name; world_suffixes only as a world name's last word (Cedar Creek Park is a fine park). The Rusty-<thing> and St.-Jude shapes are matched in code (xeric_forge_place_name_ok), because a regex in a data file fails silently and these two must not.
